slides: Your strength stalls not because you’re lazy, but because you never add micro‑load.
A micro‑load is 0.5‑2 kg or 1‑2 % more volume on a set you already master.
The nervous system adapts to any perceived novelty, however tiny.
Add that extra weight or rep every 3‑4 workouts and you force a fresh adaptation.
Result: steady gains without the injury spikes of big jumps.
Discipline collapses when your actions drift from your core values.
Values are the compass; actions are the steps you take on the map.
When a task doesn’t point toward a value, the brain tags it as expendable.
Audit your daily to‑do list: match each item to a top‑3 value.
If it doesn’t align, drop it—your discipline budget stays intact.
Energy isn’t a tank you fill once; it’s a wave you can surf.
Cortisol peaks in the early morning, testosterone climbs mid‑day, and melatonin rises at night.
Schedule high‑intensity work when testosterone is highest, and creative tasks when cortisol eases.
A brief 10‑minute walk after lunch resets the wave, preventing the midday slump.
Ride the natural rhythm and you’ll produce more output with less fatigue.
Habit stacking fails when the anchor habit is frictionless.
Friction is the tiny obstacle that makes you pause and notice the next step.
Add a deliberate hurdle—like putting your running shoes on the other side of the room.
That extra step forces a mental cue, turning a vague intention into a concrete trigger.
Use friction wisely and your stacks stick without willpower battles.
